notes.meaning: Moses tells the Israelites what to do once they enter and settle in Canaan. The land is not something they earned, but an inheritance given freely by God according to His ancient promise. Settling there peacefully was proof that God keeps His word.

Once settled, each family was to gather some of the first ripe produce, place it in a basket, and bring it to God's chosen place of worship. Offering the very first part of the harvest honored God as the real owner of the land and the provider of their food. It taught the people to put God before their own appetites.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teachers claim that Christians must give financial firstfruits offerings to guarantee personal wealth and blessing.

notes.meaning: The worshipper had to go to the priest on duty and state that he had arrived in the land God swore to give their ancestors. This confession was a public testimony that the Lord is faithful and keeps His promises. It reminded the worshipper that his home was a gift of divine grace.

The priest took the basket from the worshipper's hand and placed it before the altar of the Lord. By doing this, the priest received the gift on God's behalf. It showed that the harvest came from the Lord, not from the false gods of the land.

The worshipper then recited Israel's humble beginnings, describing their ancestor Jacob as a wandering Aramean who went down to Egypt as a small group. While living there as foreigners, God multiplied them into a great, mighty, and populous nation. Remembering their weak, homeless roots kept the people humble and grateful to God.

The confession recounts how the Egyptians turned against Israel, mistreating them and forcing them into harsh slavery. The Israelites were helpless under this cruel oppression and could not free themselves.

In their misery, the people cried out to the Lord, the God of their ancestors, for deliverance. The Lord heard their cries and saw their suffering, hard labor, and distress. He showed deep mercy to an afflicted people who looked to Him for help.
God brought Israel out of Egypt by His own mighty power, using terrifying judgments, signs, and wonders. Their freedom was not won by human army or wisdom, but by the outstretched arm of the Lord.

The Lord led them through the wilderness and brought them into Canaan, a fertile land flowing with milk and honey. The worshipper gave thanks not only for his individual crops, but for the rich homeland God had provided for the entire nation.

The worshipper presented the basket of firstfruits to God and bowed down in reverent worship. Bringing the gift was only part of the duty; it had to be accompanied by a humble and thankful heart. True giving always leads to sincere adoration of the Lord.

The worshipper was told to rejoice in all the good things God had given him and his household. This celebration was not private, but was shared with the local Levite and the foreign resident living among them. God wants His people to enjoy His blessings cheerfully and generously share them with those in need.

Every third year, the special tithe (a tenth of the harvest) was kept locally instead of being taken to the central sanctuary. It was given to the Levite, foreigner, orphan, and widow so they would have plenty of food in their own towns. God commanded this practice to make sure the poor and landless were fed.

After sharing this tithe, the worshipper made a solemn declaration before God that he had completely cleaned out the sacred portion from his home. He affirmed that he had given it honestly to the poor and needy without forgetting or disobeying any command. Because no priest supervised this local giving, each person stood accountable directly before God.

The worshipper testified that he had not mishandled the holy tithe by eating it while in mourning, removing it while unclean, or misusing it for funeral practices. The dedicated food was sacred to the Lord and had to be kept pure and used with reverent obedience.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars understand 'for the dead' as referring to pagan rites of ancestor worship or leaving food in graves for the deceased.

notes.meaning: Having faithfully managed the sacred tithes, the worshipper asked God to look down from heaven and bless Israel and the land. Obeying God's commands gave the people confidence to pray for His continued favor. This prayer reminded them that even a fertile land will not produce without God's blessing.

Moses reminded the Israelites that these laws were given by God's divine authority, not by human invention. The people were urged to obey them wholeheartedly, with deep sincerity rather than out of mere outward routine.

The people publicly declared that the Lord was their God and promised to walk in His ways and keep His statutes. By doing so, they willingly entered into a sacred covenant (a binding agreement) with Him. Taking the Lord as God means committing to obey His voice.

The Lord also declared that Israel was His own treasured possession, just as He had promised, and called them to obey all His commandments. This covenant created a mutual bond between God and His people. God took them as His own special treasure so they would live holy lives for Him.

God promised to give Israel honor, praise, and renown above all other nations on earth. Their true glory would come not from military might, but from being a holy people dedicated entirely to the Lord.
